newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary APV to top up angry power workers' wages.
newsitem.headline: Hungary APV to top up angry power workers' wages.

text.p: Hungary's privatisation agency APV said on Wednesday it would offer an extra three percent pay increase for 1996 to electricity workers in companies in which it has a majority stake.
"We will offer three percent on top of the rise they have received for 1996 in the form of a one-off payment," APV spokesman Adam Dudits told Reuters. @

The Electricity Industry Workers' Trade Union Association (VIDSZSZ) staged protests for higher wages in Germany and Belgium last Friday against Western investors in Hungary's power sector who they said had reneged on promises to keep workers' salaries in line with inflation.
The unions said employees would receive only a 19.5 percent back payment for 1996, while they were expecting 25 percent. They threatened strike action in pursuit of their claim. @
"APV is making the move to because winter is coming," Dudits said, adding that the unions had accepted the three percent and would not strike. @
However, Dudits said the agreement at this stage only applied to companies in the energy sector in which the state still has a majority holding.

These include the power supply company MVM and a number of power stations but not the regional distribution companies in which firms such as Germany's RWE and Gaz de France invested over two billion forints last year and who constituted the main target of last week's protests.
"We are not majority members of their boards so we cannot decide for them," Dudits said. @
The unions said on Monday the government had created tensions over wages which could lead to strikes in the heavily western-owned energy sector.
"I can blame the responsibility on the government and the Parliament," VDSZSZ Deputy President Gabor Major told Reuters.

Hungary was the first country in eastern Europe to sell large stakes in the energy sector to western investors one year ago, creating record privatisation revenue. The rapidness of the sales surprised many analysts and the privatisations were quoted afterwards as a success story. @
But the government disappointed western investors by cancelling an energy price rise due in October and announcing retail price hikes for January which fell short of their expectations.

The investors, claiming they would not receive the promised return, say they do not feel compelled to abide by previous agreements with the employees to keep up the real value of wages at the privatised firms in 1996, Major said.
